q: Contoso wants Defender for Endpoint to remediate confirmed threats on user workstations without waiting for approval, but every remediation on the domain controllers must stay pending until an analyst reviews it. How should you configure automated investigation and response (AIR)?
opts: Set the tenant-wide automation level to Full and rely on the Action Center history to undo unwanted server remediation afterward
Onboard the domain controllers to Defender for Identity instead, so AIR in Defender for Endpoint skips them
Place workstations and servers in separate device groups, with the Full automation level on the workstation group and a Semi level on the server group
Set the tenant-wide automation level to Semi and approve each workstation remediation from the Action Center as it appears
why: The AIR automation level is a property of a device group, so two groups can behave differently: Full for workstations, Semi (approval required) for domain controllers. A tenant-wide Full level would remediate servers first and only let you undo afterward. A tenant-wide Semi level forces manual approval for the workstations too, which is what you want to avoid. Defender for Identity covers the domain controllers' identity signals but does not change how AIR treats a device that is onboarded to Defender for Endpoint.

q: Two Sentinel automation rules are scoped to the same analytics rule. One pages the on-call analyst (order 2). Another closes incidents caused by a known vulnerability scanner as benign (order 3). The on-call analyst is still being paged for incidents that then get auto-closed. What should you change?
opts: Delete and recreate the auto-close rule, because the most recently created automation rule runs first
Rename the auto-close rule so that it sorts alphabetically ahead of the paging rule
Move the auto-close condition into the paging rule's playbook, because playbooks run before automation rules
Give the auto-close rule a lower order number than the paging rule, so it evaluates first
why: Automation rules run in ascending order number, and a rule's conditions are evaluated when its turn comes, so the auto-close rule must have the lower number to act before the paging rule. Names and creation dates play no part in ordering. Playbooks are invoked by automation rules, not ahead of them, so a check inside the playbook would run only after the page had already been requested.

q: A Sentinel playbook must, when it runs for a case, loop through every alert and every account, host and IP entity in that case and look each one up in a reputation service. Which Logic Apps trigger should the playbook use?
opts: When a response to a Microsoft Sentinel entity is triggered (entity trigger)
When a response to a Microsoft Sentinel alert is triggered (alert trigger)
When Microsoft Sentinel incident creation rule was triggered (incident trigger)
When an HTTP request is received, with the Sentinel connector added later
why: The incident trigger hands the playbook the whole incident object, from which it can pull all correlated alerts and entities. The alert trigger exposes only one alert's data, the entity trigger runs manually against a single entity from the investigation graph, and a bare HTTP trigger carries no Sentinel context unless you build it yourself.

q: Contoso must raise an incident within about a minute whenever a new member is added to a privileged Entra role. The audit events arrive in a supported table, and the detection needs only a simple query. A 5-minute scheduled rule was rejected as too slow. Which analytics rule type should you create?
opts: Near-real-time (NRT) rule
Fusion rule that correlates the audit events with other alerts
Microsoft security rule that mirrors Entra ID Protection alerts
Scheduled rule with a 1-minute frequency and a 1-minute lookback
why: NRT rules run about once a minute against a simple query on supported tables, which fits the latency need. A scheduled rule cannot be set below its 5-minute minimum frequency, so a 1-minute schedule is not an option. A Microsoft security rule only mirrors alerts another product already raised, and Fusion is an ML engine that correlates multiple weak signals rather than evaluating your own query.

q: Firewall logs reach Sentinel through the CEF connector using Azure Monitor Agent. Debug-level messages make up about 60 percent of the volume, are never queried, and drive up ingestion cost. How do you cut the cost?
opts: Add a transformation to the Data Collection Rule that drops the debug rows before ingestion
Reduce the table's retention period so the debug rows age out sooner
Create a summary rule that aggregates the raw rows into a smaller table
Add a where clause excluding debug rows to each analytics rule that reads the table
why: An ingestion-time transformation in the DCR removes rows before they are stored, so they are never billed as ingestion. Filtering in analytics rules changes what a query returns but the full volume is still ingested. Retention affects how long data is kept, not what is charged at ingestion. A summary rule creates an additional table from data already ingested, so the raw volume is still paid for.

q: A CISO wants a matrix view of which MITRE ATT&CK techniques currently have no enabled analytics rule or hunting query in the Sentinel workspace, to decide where detection engineering effort should go next. Which should the SOC use?
opts: Threat analytics in the Microsoft Defender portal
The Analytics efficiency workbook
The regulatory compliance dashboard in Defender for Cloud
The MITRE ATT&CK page in Microsoft Sentinel
why: The MITRE ATT&CK page maps the workspace's own rules and queries to techniques and shows where nothing covers a technique. Threat analytics reports on specific named threats and whether you are exposed to them. The Analytics efficiency workbook measures how well existing rules perform, not technique coverage. The regulatory compliance dashboard maps Azure resource configuration to named standards, not ATT&CK.

q: In advanced hunting, an analyst uses Security Copilot to generate a KQL query from a plain-language description and now wants to turn it into a custom detection rule that runs on a schedule. What should the analyst do first?
opts: Recreate the query by hand, because a Copilot-generated query is not accepted by custom detections
Save it directly as a rule, because Copilot validates generated queries against the schema and tenant data
Run the query and review its logic and results to confirm it finds the intended behavior
Ask Copilot to confirm the query's accuracy, then publish without running it
why: Security Copilot accelerates drafting, but the analyst remains responsible for confirming the query does what was intended before it becomes an automated detection. Schema validity does not prove the logic is right or that false positives are acceptable. Asking Copilot to grade its own output is not independent validation. There is no restriction that stops a generated query from backing a custom detection once it has been reviewed.

q: HR sends a weekly CSV of about 300 terminated employees' UPNs. Sentinel analytics rules must alert on any sign-in by these accounts, and the SOC wants to replace the list each week without editing any rule's KQL. What should you use?
opts: A dynamic array defined in a let statement at the top of each rule
A Sentinel watchlist, referenced in the rules with the _GetWatchlist() function
Threat intelligence indicators imported through the threat intelligence blade
A workbook parameter populated from the CSV
why: A watchlist is analyst-curated reference data imported from CSV and queried with _GetWatchlist(), so refreshing the list requires no change to the rules. Threat intelligence indicators describe threat artifacts such as malicious IPs, domains and hashes, with confidence and expiry, not an HR roster. A let array would have to be edited in every rule. A workbook parameter exists only inside a workbook and cannot feed an analytics rule.

q: On a user's entity page, Sentinel shows that she accessed a SharePoint site for the first time and that no one else in her peer group has ever touched it. No analytics rule is configured for this activity. Which feature produced the finding?
opts: The Microsoft security analytics rule type
A scheduled rule joined to a watchlist of SharePoint sites
Fusion advanced multistage attack detection
User and Entity Behavior Analytics (UEBA)
why: UEBA builds baselines per entity and against its peer group, then surfaces first-time or unusual activity as enrichment without any rule being authored. Fusion correlates several lower-fidelity alerts into one incident and needs alerts to exist. A scheduled rule with a watchlist would need someone to write it. The Microsoft security rule type only turns another product's existing alerts into incidents.

q: A SOC installs a content hub solution for a new firewall vendor. The data connector shows data arriving and the table is populated, but a week later there are no incidents from it. Which should you check first?
opts: Whether the solution's data connector DCR has a transformation that removes the alert fields
Whether analytics rules were actually created from the solution's rule templates and are enabled
Whether the lookback of the solution's workbook is long enough to show historical alerts
Whether the workspace's UEBA baseline has finished syncing for the firewall's devices
why: Installing a solution stages its analytics rule templates; nothing generates incidents until a rule is created from a template and enabled. A DCR transformation could hide fields, but that is a less likely cause than rules never being enabled. UEBA baselines do not gate analytics rules, and a workbook only visualizes data and has no effect on incident creation.

q: A scheduled rule is configured to group alerts into one incident when the Account entity matches. Two alerts minutes apart concern the same user, yet they create two separate incidents. The query output includes the user's UPN in a plain column. What should you do?
opts: Extend the rule's query lookback to the maximum of 14 days
Map that column to the Account entity in the rule's entity mapping
Set event grouping to trigger a single alert for all events
Add an automation rule that merges incidents with the same owner
why: Alert grouping compares mapped entities, so a UPN that is not mapped to an Account entity cannot be matched across alerts. Event grouping controls how many alerts a single query run produces, not whether separate alerts merge into an incident. Query lookback changes which events are scanned, not how alerts are grouped. Automation rules can change owner and severity but are not the mechanism for merging alerts by entity here.

q: A vulnerability scanner's IP addresses change every month and IT maintains the current list. A brute-force analytics rule keeps raising false positives from them. You want these sources excluded so no alert or incident is created, without editing the rule when the list changes. What should you do?
opts: Hardcode the current scanner IPs in the rule query and update them each month
Create an automation rule that closes the resulting incidents as benign
Enable alert suppression on the rule for 24 hours
Keep the scanner IPs in a watchlist and exclude them via _GetWatchlist()
why: Excluding a watchlist in the query stops the alerts from being generated and lets IT change the list without touching the rule. Hardcoded addresses work today but require a rule edit every month. An automation rule closes incidents that were still created, leaving alert noise and wasted triage. Suppression only pauses the rule temporarily and for all sources, not just the scanner.

q: A SOC subscribes to a TAXII feed of malicious IP addresses. Each indicator has a confidence score and expires after 30 days. Detections must match sign-in IPs against these indicators and ignore expired ones. Which approach fits?
opts: Import the feed as threat intelligence indicators and use the TI-based analytics rule templates
Import the feed as a watchlist and join it with _GetWatchlist() in a scheduled rule
Add the feed's IP addresses as a custom indicator in Defender for Endpoint
Ingest the feed into a custom _CL table and write a separate rule for each indicator type
why: Threat intelligence indicators carry confidence and validity dates, land in the ThreatIntelIndicators table (which replaced the legacy ThreatIntelligenceIndicator table), and are matched by built-in TI analytics rule templates that honor expiry. A watchlist is static reference data with no concept of indicator expiry or confidence. A custom table duplicates what the TI blade already provides. A Defender for Endpoint indicator blocks or alerts on devices but does not match Entra sign-in logs in Sentinel.

q: A SOC manager wants a live dashboard of incident volume and mean time to close for executives with Reader access, and also wants someone alerted whenever mean time to close exceeds four hours. Which design meets both needs?
opts: A playbook for the dashboard, plus an automation rule for the threshold alert
A workbook for the dashboard, plus a scheduled analytics rule over SecurityIncident for the threshold alert
A single workbook that also generates incidents when a tile crosses the threshold
A hunting query bookmark for the dashboard, plus a saved hunting query run each morning for the threshold alert
why: Workbooks visualize KQL results for human readers but cannot raise incidents themselves, so the alerting need requires a scheduled analytics rule querying SecurityIncident. A playbook performs actions and does not render dashboards, and an automation rule reacts to incidents rather than measuring a metric. Bookmarks preserve hunting evidence, and a saved hunting query is run by hand and raises no alert on its own.

q: Automatically closing a Sentinel incident that matches a known-benign pattern requires a playbook, because automation rules cannot change an incident's status on their own.
opts: True
False
why: Automation rules can change status, close an incident with a classification, assign an owner, change severity, add tags and add tasks without invoking any playbook. A playbook is needed only when the response calls an external system or does something an automation rule has no built-in action for.

q: A near-real-time (NRT) analytics rule in Sentinel runs on a fixed interval of about one minute, rather than letting you pick a query frequency the way a scheduled rule does.
opts: True
False
why: NRT rules are built for low latency: they run roughly once a minute with a fixed cadence, which is why they accept only simpler queries on supported tables. A scheduled rule lets you set its own frequency and lookback, with a minimum of five minutes.

q: Shortening a Log Analytics table's retention period is an effective way to lower the ingestion charge for the data the table receives.
opts: True
False
why: Ingestion is billed on the volume of data accepted into the workspace, and retention only controls how long stored data is kept. To lower the ingestion charge you have to ingest less, for example by filtering rows or dropping columns with a Data Collection Rule transformation, or by choosing a cheaper table plan where its limits are acceptable.

q: A Sentinel analytics rule can show as enabled with no errors and still never create an incident, simply because the table its query reads has no data.
opts: True
False
why: A rule only evaluates the query it is given. If the connector for its source table is missing or misconfigured, the query returns nothing and the rule stays silent without reporting a failure. Checking data connector health and table contents is a standard first step when an enabled rule seems dead.

q: When the contents of a Sentinel watchlist change, every analytics rule that references the watchlist must be edited and re-saved before it uses the new data.
opts: True
False
why: Rules reference a watchlist by its alias through _GetWatchlist(), and the function reads the watchlist's current contents each time the query runs. Updating the watchlist therefore changes rule behavior without touching any rule, which is the main reason to prefer a watchlist over values hardcoded in KQL.

q: UEBA can show an entity's activity compared with its peer group on the entity page even when no analytics rule has ever fired for that entity.
opts: True
False
why: UEBA builds baselines from ingested data for each user and device and compares them with peers, independent of analytics rules. The enrichment appears on entity pages and in incidents, which is why it can highlight unusual behavior that no static rule was written to catch.

q: Which two statements about Sentinel automation rules are true? (Choose two.)
opts: Adding a tag to an incident requires a playbook to be invoked by the rule
When several automation rules match an incident, they run in no defined order
A rule can trigger on incident creation and also when an incident is updated
A rule can be given an expiration date, useful for handling during maintenance
Only one automation rule can be scoped to any given analytics rule at a time
why: Automation rules support both an incident-created and an incident-updated trigger, and an expiration date lets a rule handle a short-lived situation, such as a maintenance window, without someone remembering to remove it. Tagging is a built-in rule action that needs no playbook, several automation rules can match the same analytics rule, and they run in ascending order number.

q: Which two statements about Data Collection Rules (DCRs) and Azure Monitor Agent are true? (Choose two.)
opts: A DCR transformation runs after the data is stored, so the full volume is still billed
The legacy Log Analytics (MMA) agent takes its collection settings from DCRs
One DCR can be associated with many machines, and a machine can have more than one DCR associated
A workspace transformation DCR can filter data from sources that have no DCR of their own, such as diagnostic settings
why: DCR associations are many-to-many, and the workspace transformation DCR applies transformations to tables fed by sources that do not use their own DCR. The legacy MMA agent was configured on the workspace rather than by DCRs, and a DCR transformation runs at ingestion, before storage, which is how it lowers billed volume.

q: Which two statements about the Basic Logs table plan, compared with the Analytics plan, are true? (Choose two.)
opts: Basic ingestion is billed at the same rate as the Analytics plan
Queries against Basic data are charged based on the amount of data scanned
Basic tables support the full KQL language, including joins across any table
Data on the Basic plan cannot be used as the source of a scheduled analytics rule
why: Basic Logs trades lower ingestion cost for restrictions: it cannot back analytics rules, it supports a limited KQL surface, and each query is billed on data scanned. Full KQL with arbitrary joins and the same ingestion rate describe the Analytics plan.

q:
A scheduled analytics rule contains the following KQL:

let riskyIPs = ThreatIntelIndicators
| where Confidence > 70
| project NetworkIP = ObservableValue;
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| join kind=inner riskyIPs on $left.IPAddress == $right.NetworkIP
| project UserPrincipalName, IPAddress, TimeGenerated

What does this query return?
opts: Every sign-in from the last day, annotated with a null NetworkIP column when no threat intelligence match exists
Only sign-ins from the last day whose IP address matches a high-confidence threat intelligence indicator
Every threat intelligence indicator regardless of whether any sign-in matched it
A syntax error, since join requires the left and right column names to be identical
why: kind=inner keeps only rows with a matching key on both sides, so this query returns sign-ins from the last day whose IPAddress matches a high-confidence (Confidence > 70) threat intelligence indicator value. Returning every sign-in with nulls for non-matches describes a leftouter join instead, returning every indicator regardless of a sign-in match describes a rightouter join, and join explicitly supports differently named join columns through the $left. and $right. prefixes in the on clause, so this is not a syntax error.

q: A firewall produces very high-volume debug logs that are queried only occasionally by an analyst running simple single-table searches during investigations. No detection will ever read them. The team wants the lowest practical ingestion cost. Which table plan fits?
opts: Analytics, with the logs summarized by a summary rule
Basic Logs
Analytics, with a short retention period
Analytics, with the table's data exported to long-term archive
why: Basic Logs offers cheaper ingestion for high-volume data that is searched occasionally and never needed by analytics rules. Analytics keeps full ingestion cost whatever the retention, a summary rule adds a table without avoiding ingestion of the raw rows, and archive is a retention state for older data rather than a cheaper way to ingest it.

q: A tier 1 analyst must assign, comment on, change the status of and close Sentinel incidents, but must not create or edit analytics rules or other workspace content. Which built-in role gives the least privilege that meets this?
opts: Microsoft Sentinel Reader
Microsoft Sentinel Contributor
Microsoft Sentinel Playbook Operator
Microsoft Sentinel Responder
why: Responder can manage incidents, such as assigning, commenting and closing, without being able to author analytics rules. Contributor adds rule and workbook authoring, which is more than needed. Reader can only view, and Playbook Operator exists for running playbooks and does not provide incident management.

q: Tasks on a Sentinel incident can only be added manually by an analyst after the incident exists; an automation rule has no way to add them.
opts: True
False
why: An automation rule can add a task list to an incident when it is created or updated, so every analyst gets the same checklist for a given incident type. Analysts can also add tasks manually, but automation is the usual way to standardize triage.

q: Which two statements about built-in Microsoft Sentinel roles are true? (Choose two.)
opts: Reader can close the incidents it is able to view in the workspace
Playbook Operator can edit analytics rules and automation rules
Responder can change an incident's status and assign it, but cannot edit analytics rules
Contributor can create and edit analytics rules and workbooks in the workspace
Contributor includes permission to author the Logic Apps that back playbooks
why: Responder manages incidents without authoring content, while Contributor adds authoring of analytics rules and workbooks. Reader is view-only. Building the Logic Apps behind playbooks needs Logic App permissions on the playbook's resource group, which Sentinel Contributor does not supply, and Playbook Operator is limited to running playbooks.

q: An external auditor must read only the AuditLogs table in the Sentinel workspace and nothing else, including other tables and incidents. How should access be granted?
opts: A custom role scoped to the workspace with read on only the AuditLogs table
Assign the Log Analytics Reader role on the resource group that contains the workspace
Assign the Microsoft Sentinel Reader role on the workspace to the auditor's account
Assign the Microsoft Entra Security Reader role to the auditor's account in the tenant
why: Table-level RBAC lets a custom role grant read access to a named table in a workspace. Sentinel Reader and Log Analytics Reader both expose data across the workspace rather than a single table. The Entra Security Reader role covers Entra security information and does not scope access to one Log Analytics table.

q: A Data Collection Rule must drop incoming rows whose Severity column equals 'Debug' before they are stored. Which transformKql in the DCR achieves this?
opts: source | where Severity != 'Debug'
source | summarize count() by Severity
source | project-away Severity
AppAudit_CL | where Severity != 'Debug'
why: A DCR transformation reads the incoming stream as source, and a where clause removes the unwanted rows before storage. Referencing the destination table name is not how a transformation addresses its input. project-away removes a column but keeps every row, and summarize collapses the data into counts and loses the detail you meant to keep.

q: An automation rule with the 'When incident is created' trigger sets the owner and severity of new incidents. Later, an analyst raises an incident's severity to High, and the SOC wants a playbook to notify management at that moment. What should you do?
opts: Change the analytics rule's alert grouping so a severity change creates a new incident
Create another automation rule with the 'When incident is updated' trigger and a condition on the severity change
Attach an alert-trigger playbook to the analytics rule, which fires when incident severity changes
Add the notify action to the existing creation rule, which re-evaluates whenever an incident changes
why: A rule on the incident-created trigger evaluates only when the incident is created, so a later severity change needs a rule on the incident-updated trigger with a condition on that change. The creation rule does not re-run on updates. An alert-trigger playbook reacts to alerts, not to analyst edits of an incident, and alert grouping controls how alerts merge, not what happens on a severity change.

q: For a Sentinel automation rule to run a playbook, Sentinel itself must be granted permissions on the resource group that contains the playbook.
opts: True
False
why: Automation rules run playbooks under Sentinel's own service identity, so that identity needs explicit permission (the Microsoft Sentinel Automation Contributor role) on the playbook's resource group. Without it the playbook does not appear as a selectable action or fails to run, even if the analyst creating the rule has ample rights.

q: A Sentinel workspace should open an incident for every Defender for Endpoint alert of Medium severity or higher, with no KQL written for the detection itself. Which analytics rule type fits?
opts: A near-real-time (NRT) rule over the SecurityAlert table
A scheduled rule that queries SecurityAlert on a timer
Fusion, with Defender for Endpoint as its data source
The Microsoft security rule type, filtered by product and severity
why: The Microsoft security rule type turns alerts raised by a connected Microsoft product into incidents and lets you filter by product, severity and alert name, with no custom detection query. A scheduled or NRT rule would need a KQL query of its own, and Fusion correlates multiple weaker signals into one multistage incident rather than mirroring every alert.

q: A team wants every change to a Sentinel analytics rule reviewed in a pull request and then deployed to the workspace automatically, instead of being edited directly in the portal. Which Sentinel feature supports this?
opts: Exporting each rule as an ARM template and deploying it by hand
Content hub, installing the team's rules as a solution
Automation rules that copy approved rules between workspaces
Repositories, connected to a GitHub or Azure DevOps repository
why: Repositories connects a workspace to a source-control repository so merged content deploys through a pipeline, which provides review and automation together. Content hub installs vendor-packaged solutions rather than a team's own version-controlled content, a manual ARM export has no review gate or automatic deployment, and automation rules act on incidents, not on rule definitions.

q: Contoso wants audit logs from an Azure SQL Database (a PaaS resource) and from a SQL Server installed on an Azure VM to reach the Sentinel workspace. How should each source be connected?
opts: Diagnostic setting on the database and also on the VM
Diagnostic setting on the VM; Azure Monitor Agent with a DCR on the database
Azure Monitor Agent with a DCR on the database and also on the VM
Diagnostic setting on the Azure SQL Database; Azure Monitor Agent and DCR on the VM
why: A PaaS resource has no operating system for an agent, so its platform logs are exported with a diagnostic setting. A SQL Server on a VM produces events inside the guest operating system, which Azure Monitor Agent collects according to a DCR. The other combinations apply each method to the wrong kind of source.

q: On one VM, Defender for Cloud lists a recommendation, 'Management ports should be closed', and also a security alert, 'Suspicious RDP brute force attempt'. How should the SOC treat these two findings?
opts: Treat both as proof of compromise and isolate the VM immediately
Treat the recommendation as the incident, with the alert as supporting context
Investigate the alert as observed activity, and fix the recommendation as an exposure gap
Close the port and dismiss the alert, since closing the port resolves the attack
why: An alert records suspicious activity that Defender for Cloud actually observed and needs investigation to learn whether the attempt succeeded. A recommendation is a standing configuration gap that reduces exposure when fixed. Closing the port prevents future attempts but does not tell you whether an earlier attempt succeeded, and a recommendation is not evidence of compromise.

q: Installing Azure Monitor Agent on a Windows server is enough to start sending its Security events to the Sentinel workspace; no Data Collection Rule is required.
opts: True
False
why: Azure Monitor Agent collects nothing until a Data Collection Rule is associated with the machine and defines what to collect and where to send it. That is the key difference from the legacy Log Analytics agent, whose collection was configured on the workspace side.

q: Which two statements about Defender for Cloud's secure score and regulatory compliance dashboard are true? (Choose two.)
opts: Closing a security alert raises the secure score
The compliance dashboard maps recommendations to the controls of standards such as ISO 27001
Fixing one recommendation can raise the secure score and improve related compliance checks
A passing compliance dashboard certifies that the organization meets the whole standard
why: The dashboard reuses Defender for Cloud's recommendations as evidence against standard controls, so one fix can improve the score and the compliance view. It is an assessment aid and not a certification, and security alerts record detected activity, so closing one does not change the posture-based secure score.

q: A SOC wants to block credential theft from the lsass.exe process on endpoints, but first needs to see what the control would have blocked without interrupting users. What should it configure?
opts: A custom file indicator that is set to the Alert action
Network protection, configured in audit mode on the endpoints
The ASR rule for LSASS credential theft, in audit mode
Controlled folder access, configured in block mode on the endpoints
why: Each ASR rule targets one behavior and has its own audit, warn or block mode, which suits a staged rollout for LSASS credential theft. Controlled folder access protects folders from ransomware-style changes, network protection governs outbound connections to low-reputation destinations, and a file indicator acts on a specific file hash rather than a behavior.

q: A security team wants to prioritize patching using each device's software inventory, missing security baseline settings and known vulnerabilities, together with whether exploits are available. Which capability provides these insights?
opts: Defender for Cloud's secure score
Attack surface reduction audit reports
Sentinel UEBA investigation priority
Microsoft Defender Vulnerability Management
why: Defender Vulnerability Management assesses software inventory, baseline configuration and CVEs on endpoints and ranks remediation by exposure and threat context. Defender for Cloud's secure score evaluates cloud resource configuration, UEBA priority scores entity behavior, and ASR audit reports show which behaviors a rule would have blocked, not patch priority.

q: A dashboard needs only a per-user, per-hour sign-in count from a very large table. The team wants that aggregate computed on a schedule into a small table, so dashboard queries scan far less data. What should they configure?
opts: Moving the source table to the archive tier
A DCR ingestion-time transformation
An NRT analytics rule
A summary rule
why: A summary rule aggregates data already in the workspace on a schedule and writes the result to a small table. A DCR transformation reshapes data before it is stored and cannot aggregate what is already there. Archive stores older data cheaply but does not create an aggregate, and an NRT rule generates incidents rather than precomputed data.

q: Contoso's Sentinel costs keep rising. The CISO wants Sentinel to point out ingested data sources that no analytics rule or query uses, and to recommend detections for threat scenarios that are currently uncovered. Which feature does this?
opts: An Azure Cost Management budget alert
SOC optimization
The Workspace usage report workbook
The MITRE ATT&CK page
why: SOC optimization compares ingestion with the detections and queries that use it and recommends both cost reductions and coverage improvements. The usage workbook shows volume and cost but not detection use, the MITRE page shows technique coverage and says nothing about cost, and a budget alert only reports spending against a threshold.

q: A tenant enforces MFA for all admins and encrypts the disks on several VMs that were previously unencrypted. Which scores respond to these changes?
opts: Microsoft Secure Score reflects MFA, and Defender for Cloud's score reflects VM encryption
Neither score changes until a security alert is closed for each item
Microsoft Secure Score reflects both changes, since it covers the tenant as a whole
Defender for Cloud's secure score reflects both changes, since it rolls up Microsoft Secure Score
why: Microsoft Secure Score measures Microsoft 365 identity, device and app posture, so MFA for admins shows up there. Defender for Cloud's secure score measures Azure and multicloud resource configuration, so disk encryption shows up there. They are separate scores over different resource types, and neither depends on alerts being closed.

q: Defender for Cloud lists two low-severity recommendations: an internet-exposed VM, and a key vault holding sensitive secrets. The cloud security graph shows the VM has a network path and permissions to reach that key vault. How should this be prioritized?
opts: Rely on JIT VM access reports, which list the resources a VM can reach
Keep both low, because secure score weights each recommendation independently
Raise priority through attack path analysis, which chains the findings together
Map both to a single regulatory compliance control and treat it as one gap
why: Attack path analysis, part of Defender CSPM, links individually minor findings into a path an attacker could follow, and ranks the path higher than either finding alone. Secure score ranks recommendations individually, JIT reports describe port access rather than reachable resources, and mapping both to a compliance control does not measure exploitability.

q: Which two statements about attack surface reduction (ASR) rules and Defender Vulnerability Management are true? (Choose two.)
opts: Defender Vulnerability Management automatically patches the devices it assesses
ASR rules match a specific file hash in the way a custom file indicator does
ASR rules depend on Microsoft Defender Antivirus real-time protection being active
Each ASR rule has its own audit, warn or block setting
why: ASR rules are per-behavior controls with individual modes and rely on Defender Antivirus's real-time engine to enforce them. A file hash match is the job of a custom indicator, and Defender Vulnerability Management identifies and prioritizes weaknesses and creates remediation requests, but it does not patch devices itself.

q: The SOC wants an email only when a High severity endpoint alert appears on servers, and an email for every severity of Defender Experts activity, all tied to new and updated incidents. Where should the analyst create these rules?
opts: Settings > Endpoints > General > Email notifications, one rule per alert
In Sentinel, as an automation rule that runs a playbook to send mail
Settings > Microsoft Defender XDR > Email notifications, as incident notification rules with severity set per service source
In Threat analytics, by following each report
why: Incident notification rules can filter by service source, detection source, and device group and can set the severity separately per source, which matches the request. The Endpoints email notifications are alert-based and cover endpoint alerts only, with no per-source severity and no incident updates. A Sentinel automation rule is a workable build but not the built-in notification feature, and it would not cover Defender Experts incidents without extra work. Following threat analytics reports notifies about reports, not incidents.

q: A backup server runs an approved tool that triggers the same low-value Defender XDR alert daily. The SOC wants matching alerts hidden from the queue with no incident created, but the signal must remain searchable in advanced hunting. What should they create?
opts: An alert tuning rule with the Hide alert action, scoped to the alert's evidence conditions
A device group with the Full automation level for the backup server
A Sentinel analytics rule with alert suppression for 24 hours
A custom detection rule that deletes the alert
why: Alert tuning (formerly alert suppression) rules match conditions on the alert's evidence and can hide the alert so no incident is created while the data stays in AlertInfo and AlertEvidence. Changing the automation level affects remediation, not alert visibility. Analytics rule suppression in Sentinel pauses a single rule's query for a period and does not tune alerts from Defender products. Custom detections create alerts and cannot delete one.

q: After onboarding Sentinel to the Defender portal, a team migrating from standalone Sentinel finds that incidents from its analytics rules are grouped exactly as in the old Sentinel configuration, not merged with other Defender alerts. They now want the Defender correlation engine to also merge incidents from most of their rules. What should they do?
opts: Move the workspace to the Basic Logs plan
Disable alert grouping in every analytics rule
Create automation rules that merge incidents by owner
Change the analytics rule correlation setting to include all rules and exclude only specific ones
why: By default analytics rules are excluded from Defender correlation at the tenant level so incident behavior stays predictable after migration, and the setting can be flipped to include all rules and exclude specific ones. Basic Logs is a table plan and has no effect on correlation. Disabling alert grouping would remove the rule-level grouping rather than invite Defender merging. Merging by owner in an automation rule is not how cross-product correlation works.

q: An analyst created an IP-address indicator to block a command-and-control server in Defender for Endpoint, but connections from a managed laptop still succeed. Network protection is enabled in block mode on the laptop. What is the most likely missing setting?
opts: Custom network indicators in Settings > Endpoints > Advanced features
Hide potential duplicate device records
Restrict correlation to within scoped device groups
Automatically resolve alerts
why: IP, domain, and URL indicators are only enforced on devices when custom network indicators is turned on in the advanced features, together with network protection. The other switches change device list hygiene, alert correlation scope, and alert resolution, none of which stops a connection.

q: A threat hunter wants to capture all PowerShell script executions only from administrator workstations, beyond default endpoint telemetry, and store them in Microsoft Sentinel for hunting without collecting every event on every device. What should you configure?
opts: An ASR rule that audits script execution
A custom data collection rule in Defender for Endpoint scoped to devices with a dynamic tag
A summary rule that aggregates DeviceProcessEvents
A Windows Event Forwarding subscription on each workstation
why: Custom data collection rules add targeted event collection with filters and device scope based on dynamic tags and send the data to a connected Sentinel workspace. An ASR rule audits or blocks behavior but does not create new collected telemetry for hunting. A summary rule aggregates data you already ingest. WEF on every workstation would be an unrelated, heavier mechanism for Windows event logs rather than Defender endpoint telemetry.

q: A company must keep identity sign-in telemetry for seven years for audits, only ever querying it occasionally for investigations, and wants the lowest practical storage cost. Detection rules need only the last 90 days. What should you configure?
opts: Keep everything in the Analytics tier with seven years of analytics retention
Set the table to the Basic Logs plan and write analytics rules against it
Keep 90 days in the Analytics tier and extend total retention in the data lake tier to seven years
Export the data monthly to a storage account and delete it from the workspace
why: Analytics tier data is mirrored to the lake, and total retention in the lake can extend to 12 years at low cost, so detections use the analytics window and audits query the lake with KQL jobs. Analytics retention is capped at two years and is the expensive hot tier. Basic Logs data cannot back analytics rules. A manual storage export loses native querying and adds operational work.

q: A junior analyst needs to run KQL jobs across all workspaces in the Sentinel data lake and write the results to the analytics tier, with the least privilege. Which role should be assigned?
opts: Microsoft Sentinel Reader at subscription level
Microsoft Sentinel Automation Contributor
Security Reader in Microsoft Entra ID
Security Operator in Microsoft Entra ID
why: The data lake uses Microsoft Entra roles, and writing job output to the analytics tier requires Security Operator, Security Administrator, or Global Administrator, Security Operator being the least privileged. Security Reader can read across the lake but not write. Sentinel Reader and Automation Contributor are Azure roles for the SIEM workspace and do not grant lake-wide write access.

q: An organization has a large fleet of servers where the Azure Monitor Agent cannot be installed on each machine, but the servers already forward Windows events to a central collector with subscriptions. How should the security team get these events into Sentinel?
opts: Install the Azure Monitor Agent with a DCR on the event collector
Create a diagnostic setting on each server
Use the Syslog via AMA connector on the collector
Ingest the events with the Azure Activity connector
why: Windows Event Forwarding centralizes events on a Windows Event Collector server, so one agent there, with a data collection rule, can ship them. Diagnostic settings apply to Azure resources, not to Windows event logs on servers. Syslog is a Linux and appliance log format. The Azure Activity connector carries Azure control-plane events, not Windows logs.

q: Security wants the diagnostic logs of every new Azure Key Vault and storage account sent to Sentinel automatically as they are created, without configuring a diagnostic setting on each resource. What should the team use?
opts: An Azure Policy assignment from the connector that applies the log-streaming configuration at the chosen scope
A manual diagnostic setting on each resource after creation
A scheduled analytics rule that queries for new resources
A Defender for Cloud secure score recommendation
why: The Azure resource connectors use Azure Policy to apply one log-streaming configuration to existing and future resources of a type within a scope, which needs the Owner role on that scope. Manual settings do not scale to new resources. An analytics rule reads data already ingested and cannot create diagnostic settings. A secure score recommendation is a posture suggestion, not a log pipeline.

q: A KQL job promoted lake data to the analytics tier overnight, and the analyst wants to know what to look for in the workspace. What best describes the result?
opts: The data is hidden until an administrator approves it
A new custom table in the analytics tier whose name ends in _KQL_CL, or rows appended to an existing table
A new Basic Logs table that cannot be queried with joins
A summary rule that reruns every 20 minutes
why: KQL jobs can write to a new analytics-tier table, suffixed _KQL_CL, or append to an existing table, and the analyst can then hunt and alert on it in the advanced hunting editor. There is no approval step. The output is analytics tier, not Basic Logs. A summary rule is a different feature with its own schedule.

q: Which two statements about Defender XDR alert tuning are true? (Choose two.)
opts: Hiding an alert prevents incident creation but the data remains in AlertInfo and AlertEvidence
Set as behavior keeps matching signals out of the alert queue while the data remains available in BehaviorInfo and BehaviorEntities
Alert tuning rules also suppress alerts raised by custom detection rules
A built-in alert tuning rule permanently stops any related automated investigation
why: Hide alert and Set as behavior both remove noise from the queue while keeping data for hunting, in different tables. Built-in tuning rules do not apply to alerts from custom detection rules or custom threat intelligence, so tune the detection itself instead. Built-in rules suppress alerts without stopping automated investigations, and a suppressed alert is reactivated if an investigation finds malicious activity.

q: Any user with the Microsoft Sentinel Responder role can read and write across all tables in the Sentinel data lake.
opts: True
False
why: The Sentinel SIEM uses Azure RBAC roles such as Responder, which manage incidents in the workspace. Lake-wide read and write access comes from Microsoft Entra roles: reads from Global Reader, Security Reader, Security Operator, or Security Administrator, and writes from Security Operator, Security Administrator, or Global Administrator.

q: Custom data collection rules in Defender for Endpoint can target devices using manually applied static tags.
opts: True
False
why: The feature requires dynamic tags configured in asset rule management and run at least once. Manual (static) tags are not supported for scoping the rule.

q: A SOC wants an agent that triages user-reported phishing emails at scale with a natural-language rationale for each verdict, without writing playbooks. Which approach fits, and what does it need?
opts: A Logic Apps playbook on the alert trigger, which needs the Playbook Operator role
The Phishing Triage Agent from the Security Store, which needs Security Copilot capacity (SCUs) and Defender for Office 365 Plan 2
A Sentinel workbook that scores emails daily
An ASR rule that blocks Office applications from creating child processes
why: The Phishing Triage Agent is a Security Copilot agent deployed from the Security Store in the Defender portal, runs autonomously with an agent identity, explains its verdicts, and needs Security Copilot capacity and Defender for Office 365 Plan 2. A playbook would need building and cannot reason about intent. A workbook only visualizes data, and an ASR rule hardens endpoints against child processes rather than triaging reported mail.

q: A developer wants an AI coding client in Visual Studio Code to answer natural-language questions about long-term security data in the Sentinel data lake, with no custom API integration and without the developer knowing the table schemas. What should be used?
opts: The Sentinel MCP server's data exploration tools
A saved hunting query in a workbook
A Jupyter notebook that the developer maintains
A scheduled analytics rule that runs hourly
why: The hosted Sentinel MCP server exposes scenario-focused tool collections that let MCP-capable clients explore data lake data in natural language and handle schema discovery themselves. A workbook or analytics rule is fixed content someone must author. A notebook can query the lake but needs code and schema knowledge from the developer.

q: A sales rep's Windows laptop is compromised. The rep must stay on a customer Teams call and keep reading mail in Outlook, while the SOC cuts the device off from everything else and keeps Defender for Endpoint telemetry flowing. Which response should the analyst use?
opts: Use the isolation option that still allows Outlook, Teams and Skype for Business
Apply Restrict app execution so only Microsoft-signed apps can run on the laptop
Use full isolation, which keeps just the connection to Defender for Endpoint
Apply the Contain device action, which restricts communication with the laptop
why: Selective isolation is the isolation option that keeps Outlook, Teams and Skype for Business connectivity while blocking other traffic, and the device stays connected to the Defender for Endpoint service. Full isolation would drop the call and mail. Contain device is meant for devices that are not onboarded, and Restrict app execution limits which apps may run without cutting off the network.

q: An analyst must run one of the team's prepared scripts on a flagged server, then download one specific file from it, immediately and without waiting for any automated process. Which Defender for Endpoint capability fits?
opts: Run antivirus scan
Initiate automated investigation
Collect investigation package
Live response
why: Live response opens an interactive remote shell on the device where the analyst can run uploaded scripts, fetch a chosen file and stop processes. Collecting an investigation package gathers a fixed set of forensic data into an archive but offers no commands. An antivirus scan only scans, and an automated investigation follows its own playbook rather than the analyst's commands.

q: At the Full automation level, AIR quarantined a legitimate internal tool on 40 devices yesterday. The tool must be restored, and it must not be flagged again. What should the analyst do?
opts: Switch the device group to a Semi level and rerun the automated investigation on the devices
Undo the quarantines from Action Center history and add an allow indicator for the hash
Delete the alert that triggered the automated investigation, which reverses its actions
Reject the quarantine actions in the Action Center's pending actions list for the device group
why: Completed remediation shows in the Action Center history, where supported actions such as quarantine can be undone, and an allow indicator for the hash keeps the file from being flagged again. The actions are no longer pending, so there is nothing left to reject. Changing the automation level affects future investigations without restoring the file, and deleting an alert reverses nothing.

q: A custom indicator set to Block for a malicious domain works in Microsoft Edge, but users on Google Chrome can still browse to it. What must be enabled so the block also applies to Chrome?
opts: A Safe Links policy covering the domain
An allow indicator for the Chrome executable
Cloud-delivered protection in Microsoft Defender Antivirus
Network protection in block mode on the devices
why: Domain and IP indicators are enforced through SmartScreen in Edge and through network protection for other browsers, so network protection in block mode is needed for Chrome. Cloud-delivered protection supports file indicators, Safe Links is a Defender for Office 365 control for links in messages and Office apps, and allowing the Chrome executable does nothing to restrict a destination.

q: A phishing campaign was reported after many messages had already reached mailboxes. An analyst must find every recipient and the delivery location of each message by sender and subject, then soft-delete the messages from the mailboxes. Which tool fits?
opts: Threat Explorer in Defender for Office 365
The Submissions page in the Defender portal
Attack simulation training in Defender for Office 365
Message trace in the Exchange admin center
why: Threat Explorer searches delivered mail by sender, subject and delivery action, and lets the analyst start remediation such as soft delete straight from the results. Message trace shows routing but offers no remediation. Attack simulation training sends practice phishing to users, and the Submissions page lists what users or admins reported, not an investigation across mailboxes.

q: A message looked clean when delivered, but updated signatures later classified it as malware. It was moved from the inbox to quarantine without any analyst approving an action. Which capability moved it?
opts: Threat Explorer with a remediation action
Automated investigation and response in Defender for Office 365
Zero-hour auto purge (ZAP)
Safe Attachments Dynamic Delivery
why: ZAP acts automatically on already-delivered mail whose verdict changes after delivery. Automated investigation in Defender for Office 365 produces recommended actions that typically wait in the Action Center for approval. Dynamic Delivery works before delivery by holding the attachment while scanning, and Threat Explorer remediation is started by an analyst.

q: Defender for Identity flags a chain of computers and cached credentials an attacker could use to eventually reach a Domain Admin account, even though no attack is currently in progress. What is this finding called, and what does it represent?
opts: A lateral movement path -- a proactive exposure finding showing what a compromise could reach, not an active attack
A honeytoken alert -- a high-confidence signal that a decoy account was touched, not a mapped chain of reachable credentials
A Fusion incident -- a machine-learning correlation of several lower-fidelity alerts into one higher-confidence case
A regulatory compliance failure -- a gap against a specific standard's control requirement, unrelated to credential exposure
why: A lateral movement path is a proactive, exposure-focused finding mapping what an attacker could reach through cached credentials, distinct from an alert about an attack already happening. A honeytoken alert or Fusion incident would instead reflect actual observed malicious activity, and this has nothing to do with a compliance standard.

q: Contoso creates an enabled account named svc-backup-old that no person or service should ever use. Defender for Identity must raise a high-confidence alert on any authentication attempt that involves it. How should the account be configured in Defender for Identity?
opts: Tag it as a sensitive account
Add it to an exclusion so activity is not noisy
Add it to the Domain Admins group for visibility
Tag it as a honeytoken account
why: Tagging an unused decoy account as a honeytoken makes any activity involving it an alert, since no legitimate user has a reason to touch it. A sensitive tag marks high-value accounts such as admins to extend detections and lateral movement path analysis, an exclusion suppresses detections, and adding an unused account to Domain Admins creates risk without producing detections.

q: An organization wants to block a user from downloading a file from a sanctioned cloud app during an active, already-authenticated session, based on real-time conditions like an unmanaged device. Which capability enforces this?
opts: A Conditional Access App Control access policy, evaluated only at sign-in before the session starts
A Sentinel automation rule triggered on incident creation
Defender for Endpoint live response targeting the user's device directly
Conditional Access App Control with a session policy
why: Conditional Access App Control routes the session through Defender for Cloud Apps as a reverse proxy, and a session policy can then enforce real-time, in-session controls like blocking a download. An access policy only gates whether the session is allowed to start, not what happens inside it once authenticated, and a Sentinel automation rule or Defender for Endpoint live response operate on incidents and endpoints, not live in-session cloud app enforcement.

q: Contoso wants Defender for Cloud Apps to alert when any single user downloads more than 30 files from SharePoint Online within five minutes, using thresholds the SOC chooses. Which policy type should be created?
opts: An anomaly detection policy
A session policy
A file policy
An activity policy
why: Activity policies let you define the activity, the count threshold and the time window yourself. Anomaly detection policies, such as impossible travel, use built-in machine learning baselines and are tuned by sensitivity rather than explicit thresholds. A session policy acts on a live proxied session, and a file policy inspects file content and metadata at rest.

q: During a ransomware campaign, Defender XDR correlated signals across several workloads and, with no custom rule configured and no analyst approval, disabled the compromised account and contained the devices being used. Which capability did this?
opts: A custom detection rule with response actions
A Conditional Access sign-in risk policy
Automated investigation and response at the Full automation level
Automatic attack disruption
why: Automatic attack disruption uses high-confidence cross-workload signals to contain users and devices at machine speed. AIR investigates alerts and remediates artifacts such as files, rather than containing accounts across an incident. A custom detection rule performs actions only if someone built it, and a sign-in risk policy governs future sign-ins rather than containing devices.

q: After the Microsoft Defender XDR connector is enabled in Sentinel with incident synchronization, analysts see two incidents for each Defender for Endpoint alert: one synchronized from Defender XDR and one created by Sentinel. What is the likely cause and fix?
opts: Microsoft security analytics rules also create incidents for those alerts; disable those rules
Alert grouping is set too narrow; widen the grouping time window on the rules
Fusion is correlating the alerts a second time; disable the Fusion rule
Bidirectional synchronization copies incidents instead of linking them; turn synchronization off
why: When Defender XDR incidents are already synchronized, a Microsoft security rule that creates incidents from the same product's alerts produces duplicates, so those rules should be disabled. Synchronization links one incident across both portals and does not duplicate it, Fusion does not create incidents from every alert, and alert grouping applies only to alerts that Sentinel rules generate.

q: With selective isolation, an analyst can exempt any business application on the device, identified by its process name, so that it keeps network access while everything else is blocked.
opts: True
False
why: Selective isolation is a fixed option that keeps Outlook, Microsoft Teams and Skype for Business connected. It is not a general allow list by process name, so an arbitrary business application, such as a backup agent, would still be cut off under selective isolation. Where the newer isolation exclusions feature is enabled, admins can separately exempt specific processes, IP addresses, or services, but that is a different capability from selective isolation.

q: Zero-hour auto purge is available only to tenants licensed for Defender for Office 365; a tenant with Exchange Online Protection alone does not get it.
opts: True
False
why: ZAP is part of Exchange Online Protection as well as Defender for Office 365, and acts on malware, phishing and spam verdicts that change after delivery. The paid plans add other capabilities such as Safe Links, Safe Attachments and Threat Explorer, which are often confused with ZAP.

q: Defender for Identity can report a lateral movement path to a sensitive account even when no alert has ever been raised for any account or machine on that path.
opts: True
False
why: A lateral movement path is an exposure finding built from where privileged accounts have signed in and what an attacker could reach from a given machine. It shows an opportunity and does not depend on any alert having fired, which is why it is used to harden an environment before an attack.

q: For a Defender for Cloud Apps session policy to apply to an app, an Entra Conditional Access policy must first route the app's sessions through Conditional Access App Control.
opts: True
False
why: Session control works because a Conditional Access policy with the Use Conditional Access App Control session setting sends the user's session through the Defender for Cloud Apps reverse proxy. Without that routing, the session never reaches the proxy and a session policy has nothing to act on.

q: Safe Links in Defender for Office 365 can check URLs in Microsoft Teams messages and Office apps, not just in email.
opts: True
False
why: Safe Links protection extends beyond email to links in Teams and in Office apps, checking the destination at click time. Many people assume it is an email-only feature, but click-time checking applies wherever the policy covers the link.

q: Which two statements about Defender for Endpoint device isolation are true? (Choose two.)
opts: An isolated device is released automatically the next time it restarts
Selective isolation lets the analyst choose any process by name to keep communicating
An isolated device remains reachable for live response sessions
Selective isolation additionally lets Outlook, Teams and Skype for Business connect
why: Isolation keeps the device connected to the Defender for Endpoint service so live response and investigation continue, and selective isolation adds Outlook, Teams and Skype for Business connectivity. It is not a per-process allow list, and the device stays isolated until an analyst releases it.

q: Which two statements about zero-hour auto purge (ZAP) are true? (Choose two.)
opts: ZAP removals wait in the Action Center until a security operator approves them
ZAP acts on a delivered message when its verdict changes to malware or phishing after delivery
ZAP rewrites URLs in messages so each click is checked at the time of the click
ZAP is included with Exchange Online Protection, not only with Defender for Office 365
why: ZAP is a post-delivery control included in Exchange Online Protection that reacts when a verdict changes after delivery. Rewriting URLs for click-time checks is Safe Links, and ZAP acts automatically rather than waiting for approval, unlike many automated investigation actions.

q: Which two statements about automatic attack disruption in Defender XDR are true? (Choose two.)
opts: It requires a Sentinel automation rule to be configured before it can act
Actions it takes appear in the Action Center, where an analyst can undo them
It acts on every alert in the tenant, whatever the confidence level
It relies on signals correlated across several Defender workloads to reach high confidence
why: Attack disruption works from correlated high-confidence signals and records its containment actions so they can be reviewed and reversed. It is built into Defender XDR and does not depend on Sentinel, and it is deliberately limited to high-confidence attack patterns, not every alert.

q: A query in Defender XDR advanced hunting reliably finds a malicious process pattern on endpoints. The SOC wants it to run on a schedule and automatically isolate any device that matches, using only features inside the Defender portal and no playbook. What should the analyst do?
opts: Create a Defender for Cloud Apps activity policy that targets the same pattern
Create a custom detection rule from the query with the isolate device response action
Create a Sentinel scheduled analytics rule and attach a playbook that isolates the device
Save the query as a bookmark so matches can be reviewed later
why: A custom detection rule runs a hunting query on a schedule, raises alerts, and can take response actions such as isolating a device, all within Defender XDR. A Sentinel rule would need a playbook for the isolation, which the scenario excludes. A bookmark only preserves results, and activity policies watch cloud app activity rather than endpoint processes.

q: Users complain that email delivery is delayed while attachments are scanned for malware, but security still wants every attachment scanned before a recipient can open it. Which Safe Attachments setting addresses both concerns?
opts: Block delivery until scanning completes, holding the entire message including the body until the attachment clears
Dynamic Delivery, which delivers the message body immediately and makes the attachment available once scanning finishes
Monitor-only mode, which logs suspicious attachments for later review without blocking or delaying delivery
Disabling Safe Attachments and relying on zero-hour auto purge to catch anything malicious after the fact
why: Dynamic Delivery delivers the email body to the recipient right away while the attachment continues scanning in the background, then makes the attachment available once scanning completes -- addressing the delay complaint while still ensuring every attachment is scanned before it can be opened. Blocking delivery until scanning completes is exactly the delay users are complaining about, monitor-only mode does not scan-and-hold at all, and disabling Safe Attachments in favor of ZAP would remove pre-open scanning entirely, relying only on a post-delivery reclassification.

q: Contoso wants to be alerted, and have the app disabled automatically, whenever an OAuth app that holds Mail.Read suddenly makes an unusually high number of Microsoft Graph calls. Which capability fits?
opts: An app governance policy
A Defender for Cloud Apps session policy
An Entra ID Protection risky user policy
An Entra admin consent workflow
why: App governance policies watch the behavior of OAuth apps, such as a spike in Graph calls against granted permissions, and can alert on it or disable the app. Risky user policies respond to user risk, a session policy controls a live user session, and a consent workflow decides whether to approve new consent requests before access is granted.

q: Safe Attachments Dynamic Delivery delivers the message with its original attachment attached, relying on zero-hour auto purge to remove the attachment if scanning finds malware.
opts: True
False
why: Dynamic Delivery delivers the message body immediately with a placeholder where the attachment will go, and attaches the real file only after scanning finds it safe. The original attachment is never opened by the recipient before the scan completes, so it does not depend on ZAP to clean up afterward.

q: A compliance auditor needs to browse Sentinel incidents, workbooks and logs and run queries, but must not be able to change an incident's status or assign it. Which built-in role gives the least privilege that works?
opts: Microsoft Sentinel Contributor
Microsoft Sentinel Responder
Microsoft Entra Security Administrator
Microsoft Sentinel Reader
why: Sentinel Reader allows viewing incidents, workbooks and data without modifying incidents. Responder can change status and assign owners, Contributor adds content authoring, and an Entra Security Administrator role grants far broader rights in Entra security settings than the auditor needs.

q: An analyst suspects business email compromise. Which two findings, taken together, most strongly point to a compromised account rather than normal user behavior? (Choose two.)
opts: A rule forwarding mail containing 'invoice' to an external domain and marking originals as read
The mailbox size grew by a few percent over the past month, in line with earlier months
A successful MFA sign-in from an unfamiliar country, then a new inbox rule created in that session
A rule moving newsletters into a folder, created from the user's managed corporate laptop
why: A sign-in from an unusual location that is quickly followed by a rule created in that session, together with a rule that silently forwards financial mail outside the company and hides the originals, form the classic BEC pattern. Gradual mailbox growth and a newsletter rule from a managed device are ordinary behavior.

q: In a Sentinel workspace with the Microsoft 365 and Entra ID connectors enabled, which two statements about hunting for malicious inbox rules are true? (Choose two.)
opts: OfficeActivity records Exchange audit operations such as New-InboxRule
AuditLogs records Exchange mailbox rule changes made by users and admins
EmailEvents is the table where mailbox inbox rule creation is recorded
SigninLogs can be correlated with OfficeActivity on the user's UPN
why: OfficeActivity carries Exchange audit operations including inbox rule creation, and joining it to SigninLogs on the user's identity ties a rule to the sign-in that created it. EmailEvents describes message delivery, and AuditLogs holds Entra directory changes, not mailbox rules.

q: A team wants RDP on an Azure VM blocked by default, and opened only for the requester's own IP address, for a limited time, after the request is approved. Which capability fits?
opts: An Azure Firewall DNAT rule that publishes RDP to the VM
Just-in-time (JIT) VM access
Azure Bastion deployed in the VM's virtual network
A network security group rule that allows the corporate IP range
why: JIT VM access keeps management ports closed and opens them temporarily for an approved request from a specific source IP. Bastion avoids exposing RDP publicly but does not provide time-boxed, per-request approval. A standing NSG rule or firewall DNAT rule leaves the port open all the time.

q: Defender for Cloud is connected to Defender XDR. A VM has a recommendation, 'Machines should have vulnerability findings resolved', and a security alert, 'Suspicious process executed'. Which of these appears in the Defender XDR incident queue?
opts: The security alert, as a detection of observed suspicious activity
The recommendation, as a posture finding that needs triage
Neither, because Defender for Cloud findings stay in the Azure portal
Both, because Defender XDR converts each Defender for Cloud finding into an alert
why: Defender for Cloud security alerts flow into Defender XDR and can be correlated into incidents. Recommendations are posture findings that stay in Defender for Cloud and are not alerts, and Defender XDR does not turn every finding into an alert.

q: A link in a delivered email pointed to a benign page at delivery time, but the page was weaponized hours later. Which control checks the destination when the user clicks the link?
opts: A URL block entry in the Tenant Allow/Block List
Safe Links
Zero-hour auto purge
Safe Attachments Dynamic Delivery
why: Safe Links checks the destination against current intelligence at click time, which catches a page that changed after delivery. ZAP reacts to the message itself being reclassified, Dynamic Delivery scans attachments, and a block entry works only for URLs someone already knows to add.

q: When a user-risk Conditional Access policy requires a secure password change, the user must complete multifactor authentication before the password change is allowed.
opts: True
False
why: The secure password change flow first asks the user to prove who they are with MFA, so that an attacker who has the password cannot simply set a new one. This is how a risk-based policy can remediate a user without an analyst stepping in.

q: Resetting a compromised user's password immediately invalidates the refresh tokens and session cookies the attacker already holds.
opts: True
False
why: Tokens issued before the reset can keep working until they are revoked or expire. Responders therefore revoke the user's sign-in sessions as well as resetting the password, particularly after adversary-in-the-middle phishing that steals session tokens.

q: Which two statements about app governance in Defender for Cloud Apps are true? (Choose two.)
opts: It can evaluate an app's behavior after consent, such as a sudden spike in Graph API calls
It covers only apps registered in your own tenant, not third-party apps
It can disable a risky app without disabling the accounts of users who consented
It replaces Conditional Access App Control session policies
why: App governance monitors OAuth apps' permissions and behavior over time, and acts on the app itself, leaving user accounts untouched. It covers third-party apps as well as your own, and it addresses OAuth app risk, not live session control, which is the role of Conditional Access App Control.

q: A SOC needs to detect DCSync and pass-the-ticket attacks against on-premises Active Directory domain controllers. Which product provides these detections?
opts: Microsoft Defender for Office 365
Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps
Microsoft Entra ID Protection
Microsoft Defender for Identity
why: Defender for Identity monitors domain controllers and other AD infrastructure and detects on-premises attack techniques such as DCSync and pass-the-ticket. Entra ID Protection scores risk for cloud sign-ins and users, Defender for Cloud Apps watches SaaS activity, and Defender for Office 365 protects email and collaboration content.

q: On a Defender XDR incident page, an analyst wants one list of every entity and file involved, with the remediation status of each (for example, a quarantined file). Which tab fits?
opts: Activity log tab, showing actions taken
Alerts tab, listing the incident's alerts
Evidence and Response tab
Attack story tab, showing the alert timeline
why: Evidence and Response lists the entities and artifacts tied to the incident along with the remediation status of each. Attack story presents the alerts and timeline as a visual story, Alerts lists the alerts themselves, and the Activity log records what analysts and automation did to the incident.

q: Device discovery finds an unmanaged laptop, not onboarded to Defender for Endpoint, with signs of compromise. The SOC wants onboarded devices to stop communicating with it right now. What should the analyst do?
opts: Start a live response session on it
Apply the Restrict app execution action to it
Apply the Contain device action to it
Isolate the device from the network
why: Contain device is designed for devices that are not onboarded: onboarded devices block communication with the contained one. Isolation, live response and restricting app execution all act through the Defender for Endpoint agent on the target, which an unmanaged laptop does not have.

q: Contoso's authorized red team ran a phishing exercise that triggered a Defender XDR incident. How should the analyst close it so it is not counted as a real attack or as a detection error?
opts: True positive, with the phishing determination
True positive, with the multistage attack determination
False positive, with the not malicious determination
Informational, expected activity (security test)
why: The informational, expected activity classification is for real, detected activity that is authorized, such as a red-team test, and security test is its matching determination. A true positive classification counts it as a genuine attack, and false positive says the detection was wrong, which would mislead later tuning because the detection worked.

q: A first-line analyst must triage and act only on devices in a non-critical business unit, while a senior analyst keeps access to every device group. What should be configured in Defender for Endpoint?
opts: A tenant-wide automation level applied equally to the whole analyst team
Device tags that each analyst filters on when viewing the device inventory
A custom indicator limited to the first-line analyst's account
Device groups combined with role-based access control
why: RBAC roles assigned over specific device groups determine which devices an analyst can see and act on. Tags are labels used to filter and organize but do not restrict access. An automation level controls AIR's behavior, and a custom indicator blocks an artifact rather than scoping analyst permissions.

q: A factory floor has fragile OT controllers that cannot run an agent and can be disrupted by active scanning. The SOC wants anomaly and vulnerability detections for them surfaced in the unified incident queue. Which approach fits?
opts: Defender for IoT network sensors that passively monitor a mirrored copy of the traffic
Defender for Endpoint device discovery in standard mode, which probes the devices actively
Defender for Cloud Apps discovery based on firewall logs
Defender Vulnerability Management with agentless scans of each controller
why: Defender for IoT uses passive network monitoring, which is safe for fragile OT devices and needs no agent on them. Standard discovery sends probes that can disturb sensitive controllers, agentless vulnerability scanning is also active, and Cloud Apps discovery identifies SaaS usage, not OT anomalies.

q: Which two statements about Defender for Endpoint device groups are true? (Choose two.)
opts: A device can belong to several groups at once, with their settings merged
Each group has a rank, and a device is placed in the first group whose rules it matches
Device groups are used only for reporting and do not affect access or automation
A group can scope role access and also set the AIR automation level for its devices
why: Device groups are evaluated in rank order with a device landing in the first match, and a group serves both to scope RBAC and to set automation behavior. A device sits in only one group at a time, and groups do much more than reporting.

q: The SOC wants Purview Insider Risk Management alerts to show up next to related DLP and Microsoft Entra alerts in a single incident, and wants to hunt for everything the flagged user did. Where should analysts work?
opts: Only in the Purview portal, because Insider Risk alerts cannot be shown elsewhere
In the Defender portal under Incidents & alerts, where the alerts are grouped and correlated and updates stay in sync with Purview
In Sentinel workbooks, after exporting the alerts to CSV
In Microsoft Entra ID Protection risky users
why: Insider risk alerts are surfaced in the Defender portal incident and alert queues, correlated with DLP and Entra alerts, with advanced hunting by user and automatic synchronization with Purview. Restricting work to Purview loses the correlation. A CSV export is manual and stale. ID Protection tracks identity risk, not insider data activity.

q: After the built-in alert tuning rule for Purview DLP signals took effect, analysts notice DLP detections no longer create alerts or incidents in Defender XDR, although the SOC wants them. What should be done?
opts: Re-onboard the tenant to Defender for Endpoint
Disable the built-in DLP alert tuning rule under Settings > Microsoft Defender XDR > Alert tuning
Extend retention of the AlertInfo table
Create a custom detection rule on SecurityIncident
why: The built-in rule sets DLP signals as behaviors, which keeps them out of the alert queue and incident queue while leaving the data in BehaviorInfo and BehaviorEntities. Turning the rule off restores alerts. Onboarding and retention settings do not change how signals are classified, and SecurityIncident is a Sentinel table, not the place to bring back suppressed alerts.
