q: During an investigation, the team needs unified audit log entries for a mailbox rule created eight months ago. The tenant uses Purview Audit (Standard) and no add-ons. What is the outcome?
opts: The records are available because Standard keeps one year
The records are available for ten years by default
The records are gone because Standard keeps 180 days; Audit (Premium) would keep up to one year
The records can be restored from the recycle bin of the audit search tool
why: Audit (Standard) retains audit records for 180 days, and Audit (Premium) extends this to up to one year, with a ten-year add-on. Eight months is beyond Standard retention. There is no restore feature for expired audit records.

q: An investigator wants to search mailboxes and SharePoint sites for a malicious attachment name in one search and export the hits. Which statement is correct for a commercial (non-21Vianet) tenant today?
opts: Use classic Content Search, which remains the supported tool
Use classic eDiscovery (Premium), which replaced Content Search
Use the search experience in the new Purview eDiscovery, as a member of the eDiscovery Manager role group
Use the Microsoft Graph activity logs, which index mailbox content
why: All classic eDiscovery experiences, including classic Content Search, were retired on August 31, 2025 for these tenants; the same searching now lives in the new eDiscovery experience, and the eDiscovery Manager role group grants access. Graph activity logs record API requests, not mailbox content.

q: An application's service principal is suspected of reading thousands of mailboxes through the Microsoft Graph API with a stolen secret. Microsoft Entra sign-in logs show only the token requests. Which data source reveals the actual API calls?
opts: Microsoft Graph activity logs, enabled through a diagnostic setting to Log Analytics
The Entra audit log for password resets
Defender for Endpoint device timeline of the admin laptop
Sentinel UEBA anomalies for the interactive sign-ins
why: Graph activity logs record each HTTP request to the Graph service with the app, IP address, URI, and response code, which is what shows mass mailbox access, but they only exist if someone enabled the diagnostic setting beforehand. Password reset audit entries, a laptop timeline, or interactive sign-in anomalies do not capture API requests made with an application credential.

q: An analyst must see, in order, every process creation, network connection, and alert on a single compromised server, with ATT&CK techniques and the ability to flag key events. Which view fits?
opts: The device timeline in Defender for Endpoint
Threat analytics report for the campaign
The Sentinel incident tasks pane
A Defender for Cloud secure score recommendation list
why: The device timeline is the chronological per-device view of events and alerts with ATT&CK mapping, process trees, and event flagging. Threat analytics describes a campaign generally, incident tasks track analyst to-dos, and secure score lists posture recommendations.

q: Microsoft Graph activity logs are collected in every tenant by default and can be queried in Log Analytics without any setup.
opts: True
False
why: An administrator must enable them with a diagnostic setting that routes them to a destination such as a Log Analytics workspace. This requires Entra ID P1 or P2, and Security Administrator is the least privileged supported role.

q: From advanced hunting results of unusual sign-ins stored in the Sentinel data lake, an analyst wants clustering and risk scoring without writing code or KQL. Which capability should be used?
opts: A summary rule over the sign-in table
The Security Analyst Agent, started with Analyze with copilot
A watchlist of risky users
A Defender for Endpoint indicator
why: The Security Analyst Agent performs analyses such as anomaly detection, clustering, risk scoring, and forecasting on Defender, Sentinel Log Analytics, or data lake data and can be started from advanced hunting results. A summary rule only aggregates, a watchlist is static reference data, and an endpoint indicator blocks or alerts on artifacts.

q: Which two statements about Purview Audit retention are true? (Choose two.)
opts: Audit (Standard) retains audit records for 180 days
Audit (Premium) keeps records up to one year, with a longer ten-year option available
Audit must be manually turned on in every tenant before it records anything
Audit (Standard) cannot be searched with the Search-UnifiedAuditLog cmdlet
why: Standard retains 180 days; Premium extends this to up to a year with a ten-year retention option. Auditing is enabled by default, and Standard supports the audit search tool, the Search Graph API, and the Search-UnifiedAuditLog cmdlet.

q: A hunting query joins DeviceNetworkEvents (a very large table) to DeviceLogonEvents on DeviceId. Only RDP connections (RemotePort 3389) from the last day matter on the network side, and only the last day of logons. Which structure is most efficient?
opts: Filter just the logon table, because the join key already limits the network rows
Join the two full tables first, then apply the time and port filters to the joined result
Filter each table by time, and the network table by port, before the join
Join first, then use summarize to discard the rows that fall outside the filters
why: KQL runs operators in the order written, so filtering each input before the join means the join works on far fewer rows. Joining first makes the engine process the full tables, and summarize afterwards only adds work. Relying on the join key does not shrink the network table, which is the bigger side.

q: A hunting query that an analyst runs manually every week keeps finding genuine C2 beaconing. The SOC wants an incident created automatically each time it matches, with the host and IP attached as entities, and no analyst needing to remember to run it. What should the analyst do?
opts: Mark the hunting query as a favorite so it runs with the other favorites
Save the matching rows as a bookmark and add it to a new incident each week
Pin the query to a workbook tile so the team can see the matches
Create a scheduled analytics rule from the query and map the host and IP entities
why: Promoting a proven hunting query into a scheduled analytics rule makes detection automatic, and entity mapping attaches the host and IP to the incident. A bookmark preserves one set of results by hand, a workbook tile only displays results without creating incidents, and favorites only make queries easier to run manually.

q: A SOC analyst used a hunting query to find a suspicious pattern and now wants it to notify the team persistently whenever new matching events arrive, replacing the retired Sentinel livestream feature. Which approach is recommended?
opts: A bookmark on the query's current results
A scheduled or near-real-time analytics rule, with a playbook for notification
A watchlist containing the matching events
A workbook tile that is opened daily
why: Livestream is no longer available; analytics rules (and playbooks or KQL jobs) provide persistent detection and notification. A bookmark captures results that already exist, a watchlist is reference data rather than a notifier, and a workbook tile must be opened by someone to be seen.

q: A hunting query must list the accounts in a privileged-users watchlist that have no sign-in in SigninLogs over the last 7 days. The result should hold only watchlist rows, in a single join with no extra null filtering. Which join kind fits?
opts: leftanti
leftouter
leftsemi
inner
why: leftanti returns only the left-side rows that have no match on the right, which is exactly the watchlist accounts without a sign-in. leftouter keeps every left row, so you would then have to filter out the matched ones. leftsemi returns the opposite set (left rows that do match), and inner returns matched pairs only.

q: A hunting query keeps a dynamic list of suspicious executable names in a let statement. FileName values arrive in mixed case, such as PowerShell.exe and powershell.exe, and each must match a list entry exactly, ignoring case. Which filter should the query use?
opts: | where FileName in~ (suspicious)
| where FileName matches regex suspicious
| where FileName has_any (suspicious)
| where FileName in (suspicious)
why: in~ tests membership in a list and ignores case. in is case-sensitive, so PowerShell.exe would be missed if the list holds powershell.exe. has_any matches terms inside the value rather than the whole value, so it also hits names like powershell.exe.bak, and matches regex does not accept a list variable.

q: In Defender XDR advanced hunting, an analyst wants every process launched under the account of anyone who received a particular phishing email. Which join condition between EmailEvents and DeviceProcessEvents links the recipient to the process?
opts: $left.SenderFromDomain == $right.DeviceName
$left.SenderFromAddress == $right.AccountUpn
$left.RecipientEmailAddress == $right.AccountUpn
$left.NetworkMessageId == $right.ReportId
why: The recipient's email address identifies the user who received the message, and AccountUpn on the process event identifies the account that launched the process. The sender is the attacker, not the victim. NetworkMessageId and ReportId are unrelated identifiers, and a sender domain does not map to a device name.

q: An analyst's advanced hunting query ends with summarize count() by DeviceName. Saving it as a custom detection rule fails. What change makes it valid?
opts: Change DeviceName to a string literal so the output type of the query is fixed
Use arg_max so the output keeps Timestamp, ReportId and DeviceId
Add a join to the AlertInfo table so that related alerts are attached to each row
Replace summarize with project-away so that fewer columns are returned by the query
why: A custom detection needs each result row to carry Timestamp and ReportId plus a column that identifies the affected asset, such as DeviceId. A bare count by DeviceName drops those columns, so the query must preserve the event details, typically with arg_max. Removing columns, joining to alerts or hardcoding a value does not supply the required fields.

q: A KQL let variable defined in one hunting query is automatically available in every other query in the same workspace.
opts: True
False
why: A let statement is scoped to the query that contains it. To reuse the logic across queries you save it as a function, which other queries can then call by name, or keep the data in a watchlist.

q: SigninLogs and DeviceProcessEvents both record the time of each event in a column named Timestamp.
opts: True
False
why: Log Analytics tables such as SigninLogs use TimeGenerated, while Defender XDR advanced hunting tables such as DeviceProcessEvents use Timestamp. Using the wrong name in a cross-source query is a common reason a time filter errors or silently matches nothing.

q: Which two statements about KQL join kinds are true? (Choose two.)
opts: leftsemi returns columns from both tables for the rows that have a match
With no kind specified, join uses innerunique, which deduplicates left-side keys
With no kind specified, join behaves as a plain inner join over both tables
leftanti returns the left-side rows that have no match on the right
why: The default flavor is innerunique, which collapses duplicate left-side keys before matching, a frequent source of unexpectedly missing rows. leftanti keeps left rows with no match. leftsemi returns only the left-side columns, and the default is not a plain inner join.

q: Which two statements about hunting features in Sentinel are true? (Choose two.)
opts: A bookmark preserves selected result rows so they can be added to an incident as evidence
Livestream remains the primary way to get persistent notifications from a query
A bookmark re-runs its query every five minutes and updates itself
Livestream has been retired, so analytics rules, KQL jobs, or playbooks should be used for persistent notification
why: Bookmarks capture evidence from a hunt and can be attached to incidents, and livestream is no longer available, with analytics rules, KQL jobs, and playbooks as the persistent alternatives. A bookmark is a stored snapshot rather than a recurring query, so it does not re-run.

q:
A hunting query runs:

SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| summarize DistinctIPs = dcount(IPAddress) by UserPrincipalName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)

What does this return?
opts: For each user, the count of distinct IP addresses used within each 1-hour window over the last day
The total number of sign-ins for each user over the last day, with no time bucketing
A single running total of all distinct IP addresses across every user combined
Every individual sign-in row, unaggregated, sorted by IP address
why: summarize with dcount(IPAddress) computes the count of distinct IP addresses, grouped by UserPrincipalName and by bin(TimeGenerated, 1h), which buckets rows into 1-hour windows -- so the result is, per user and per hour, how many distinct IP addresses signed in. dcount specifically counts unique values rather than every sign-in (that would be count()), the grouping is per user and per hour rather than one combined running total, and summarize aggregates rows rather than returning them unaggregated.

q: In KQL, summarize by ColumnA, ColumnB with no aggregation function returns one row for each distinct combination of the two columns, the same result as distinct ColumnA, ColumnB.
opts: True
False
why: With no aggregation, summarize simply groups, so each unique combination yields one row, which is what distinct returns. distinct is the idiomatic spelling, but the two produce the same set of rows.

q: Which two statements about KQL row-limiting operators are true? (Choose two.)
opts: top works only on numeric columns and rejects datetime columns in the sort
top 10 by Timestamp desc returns the rows with the latest Timestamp
take returns an arbitrary set of rows, with no guarantee about which ones
take 10 returns the ten most recent rows by default, ordered by time
why: take is for quick sampling and gives no ordering guarantee, while top sorts by the chosen column and then returns the first N rows. take has no notion of recency, and top works on any sortable column, including datetime.

q: A query over DeviceLogonEvents in advanced hunting must return, for each device, the entire most recent logon row, including the account and logon type, not just the time. Which clause fits?
opts: | distinct DeviceName, AccountName, Timestamp
| summarize arg_max(Timestamp, *) by DeviceName
| top 1 by Timestamp desc | project DeviceName, AccountName
| summarize max(Timestamp) by DeviceName, AccountName
why: arg_max(Timestamp, *) keeps the whole row that holds the latest Timestamp in each device group. max returns only the time (plus the grouping columns) and not the rest of the row, top 1 returns a single row for the whole table rather than one per device, and distinct lists unique combinations without choosing the latest per device.

q: summarize max(TimeGenerated) by DeviceName returns the full most recent row for each device, including every other column from that row.
opts: True
False
why: max returns only the maximum value, so the output has just DeviceName and the max column. To keep the entire row that has the latest time, use arg_max(TimeGenerated, *).

q: An analyst scans 30 days of DeviceProcessEvents for command lines containing the whole term rundll32. The fastest query is wanted, and missing a longer word such as myrundll32tool is acceptable. Which expression fits?
opts: ProcessCommandLine startswith 'rundll32'
ProcessCommandLine contains 'rundll32'
ProcessCommandLine has 'rundll32'
ProcessCommandLine matches regex 'rundll32'
why: has matches whole terms using the term index, which is much faster than a substring scan and avoids matching inside longer words. contains scans substrings and would also hit myrundll32tool, a regex is slower still, and startswith misses a command line that begins with a path before the executable.

q: In a custom log table, a dynamic array column named Hashes holds four file hashes for one process launch. The analyst needs one row per hash so each can be joined to a list of indicators. Which operator should come first?
opts: | distinct Hashes
| evaluate bag_unpack(Hashes)
| mv-expand Hashes
| summarize make_list(Hashes)
why: mv-expand duplicates the row once for each array element, giving one row per hash. bag_unpack turns the keys of a property bag into columns and does not split array elements. make_list does the reverse by gathering values into an array, and distinct leaves each array intact as a single value.

q: A legacy source stores each command line as one unstructured string. A query must split the executable path and its arguments into separate columns by matching the literal text around them, without writing regular expressions. What should it use?
opts: The extract() function with a regular expression for each field
The mv-expand operator on the string column
The parse operator with literal markers between the fields
The bin() function applied to the string column
why: parse extracts several named fields from a string in one step by matching the literal text around them. extract() needs a regular expression per field, which the scenario excludes. mv-expand splits arrays, not strings, and bin() rounds numbers and times into buckets.

q: Sentinel notebooks run on Azure Machine Learning compute and let an analyst run Python, such as clustering or enrichment libraries, over data pulled from the workspace with KQL.
opts: True
False
why: Notebooks rely on an Azure Machine Learning workspace for compute and typically use libraries such as MSTICPy. They suit analysis that goes beyond KQL, such as machine learning or complex enrichment, while still querying Log Analytics data.

q: A hunt must cover data that has aged into long-term retention. Which two statements are true? (Choose two.)
opts: A search job writes its results back into the source table, replacing the original rows
Archived data can be queried directly by any KQL query with no extra step
Restoring a time range of archived data creates a restored table that can be queried like any other table until it is deleted
A search job runs asynchronously and writes the matching rows into a new table
why: Search jobs and restore are the two ways to reach long-term retention data: a search job extracts matching rows into a new table, and restore materializes a time range as a queryable table. Archived data is not directly queryable, and a search job never alters the source table.

q: A query needs rows from both DeviceProcessEvents and DeviceNetworkEvents in one result set, even though their columns differ, with a column showing which table each row came from. Which approach fits?
opts: DeviceProcessEvents | lookup (DeviceNetworkEvents) on DeviceId
union withsource=TableName DeviceProcessEvents, DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceProcessEvents | mv-expand DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceProcessEvents | join kind=fullouter (DeviceNetworkEvents) on DeviceId
why: union stacks the rows of several tables, fills missing columns with nulls, and withsource records the origin table. A full outer join pairs rows by key and widens each row instead of stacking, lookup enriches the left table with extra columns from the right, and mv-expand cannot take a table as its argument.

q: To get one column per key from a dynamic property bag, use bag_unpack; to get one row per element from a dynamic array, use mv-expand.
opts: True
False
why: The two handle different shapes of dynamic data. bag_unpack turns the keys of a property bag into columns, and mv-expand multiplies a row once for each element of an array. Using one where the other is needed leaves the nested values unusable.

q: A hunting query runs in the corporate Sentinel workspace and must also read SigninLogs from a regional subsidiary's separate workspace in the same tenant. How should the query reach it?
opts: Use the resource() function with the subsidiary's resource ID
Use the workspace() function to reference the other workspace's table
Use externaldata to read the table's exported files
Use _GetWatchlist() to import the table's contents
why: workspace('name').TableName lets one query read a table in another Log Analytics workspace, which is the standard cross-workspace pattern. resource() scopes a query to the logs of a specific Azure resource rather than naming a workspace table, externaldata reads files from storage, and _GetWatchlist() reads watchlists only.

q: During a hunt, an analyst wants to visualize how a compromised user account connects to devices and critical assets, find choke points along those paths, and act on the results, rather than writing many joins. Which tool fits?
opts: A bookmark on a SigninLogs result set
The hunting graph in advanced hunting
A summary rule over IdentityLogonEvents
A scheduled analytics rule with entity mapping
why: The hunting graph renders entity relationships interactively so analysts can trace paths and choke points. A bookmark preserves rows, a summary rule pre-aggregates data, and an analytics rule detects patterns on a schedule; none of them visualizes relationships.

q: During an active incident, the SOC lead asks which critical assets an attacker could reach from the compromised account, in addition to what is already affected. Which capability answers this most directly?
opts: Blast radius analysis in the incident graph
A UEBA anomaly report
The Action center history
A Defender for Cloud secure score recommendation
why: Blast radius analysis shows the vulnerable paths from a compromised entity to critical assets, combining current impact and possible future impact. UEBA anomalies point at unusual behavior, the Action center lists taken actions, and secure score is a posture rating.

q: A hunter must find which users clicked a malicious link delivered by email, including clicks from Teams messages and Office apps, and was told Safe Links is enabled. Which advanced hunting table should the query start from?
opts: EmailEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
UrlClickEvents
IdentityQueryEvents
why: UrlClickEvents records Safe Links clicks from email, Teams, and Office 365 apps. EmailEvents records message delivery, DeviceNetworkEvents records connections made by devices, and IdentityQueryEvents records Active Directory object queries.

q: Existing advanced hunting queries and custom detections reference the AADSignInEventsBeta table. Which statement is correct?
opts: The table is permanently kept, and no change is needed
The table is replaced by SigninLogs in advanced hunting
The table was deprecated on October 19, 2026 and queries were migrated automatically to EntraIdSignInEvents, which new queries should use
The table is replaced by EntraIdSpnSignInEvents, which holds all user sign-ins
why: AADSignInEventsBeta was deprecated on October 19, 2026 and replaced by EntraIdSignInEvents, with automatic migration of queries. SigninLogs is the Sentinel workspace table, not the advanced hunting one. EntraIdSpnSignInEvents holds service principal and managed identity sign-ins, not user sign-ins.

q: A hunter wants to run machine learning on two years of lake data to find low-and-slow lateral movement, visualizing the results with Python libraries. Which approach fits?
opts: A Jupyter notebook run through the Microsoft Sentinel extension for Visual Studio Code on Spark
A scheduled analytics rule with a 14-day lookback
A Sentinel workbook tile
A bookmark on the sign-in table
why: Data lake notebooks use PySpark and Python libraries over large historical data, which suits machine learning and visualization. A scheduled analytics rule cannot look back two years. Workbooks display results of queries and do not run models. A bookmark only saves rows that were already found.

q: For a forensic task, an analyst must pull a large volume of records from a single table, older than the date the workspace was onboarded to the data lake and now in the archive tier, into a queryable table. Which feature fits?
opts: A KQL job over the lake tier
A search job
A summary rule every 20 minutes
An automation rule
why: Search jobs reach archived data (including data older than the lake onboarding date) and hydrate large volumes from one table into a new table. KQL jobs query data from the onboarding date onward in the lake tier. Summary rules aggregate frequently, and automation rules act on incidents.

q: Which advanced hunting table records the HTTP requests that apps and users make to the Microsoft Graph API for resources in the tenant?
opts: CloudAppEvents
GraphAPIAuditEvents
AlertEvidence
DeviceEvents
why: GraphAPIAuditEvents holds Microsoft Entra ID API requests made to the Graph API. CloudAppEvents covers activity in cloud apps, AlertEvidence lists entities tied to alerts, and DeviceEvents covers endpoint events.

q: Sentinel livestream is still the recommended way to get notified as new events match a hunting query during an investigation.
opts: True
False
why: Livestream is no longer available. To automate queries and notifications, use KQL jobs, analytics rules, or playbooks, which provide persistent results and support messaging platforms.

q: Custom graphs in Microsoft Sentinel (preview) are queried with KQL on the Graphs page of the Defender portal.
opts: True
False
why: Custom graphs are published and materialized by a graph job and queried with Graph Query Language (GQL), not KQL, on the Graphs page in the Defender portal.

q: Which two statements about the Sentinel data lake and hunting are true? (Choose two.)
opts: KQL jobs can promote lake results into an analytics-tier table for further hunting
Data lake tier data supports real-time analytics rules and hunting exactly like the analytics tier
Jupyter notebooks over the lake run through the Microsoft Sentinel extension for Visual Studio Code using PySpark
Summary rules can only read from the data lake tier
why: KQL jobs can write to the analytics tier, and lake notebooks use the VS Code extension with PySpark. The lake tier is not available for real-time analytics features and hunting. Summary rules can read from Analytics, Auxiliary, Basic, and data lake tables.
